tools.title: MP4 to GIF Converter – Free, Private, No Upload
tools.description: Convert MP4 videos to high-quality animated GIFs in your browser. Trim the clip, pick width and frame rate. Your file never leaves your device.
tools.lede: Turn a clip from an MP4 video into a looping animated GIF, with optimised colours, right here in your browser.

converter.tip: GIFs get big fast. A 3–6 second clip at 480 px and 12 fps is usually a few MB.

content.heading: MP4 vs. GIF
content.html: MP4 is a modern video container, usually holding H.264 video and AAC audio. It compresses motion very efficiently, so a minute of HD footage can be just a few megabytes. GIF is a 1980s image format that stores every frame as a picture limited to 256 colours, with no sound. It is far less efficient, but it plays automatically, loops forever and works almost everywhere an image is allowed: chat apps, forums, email, documentation and slide decks.

content.heading: When to use a GIF
content.html: Choose GIF for short, silent loops: a reaction clip, a UI demo for a bug report or README, a product animation in an email newsletter, or anywhere that won't embed a video player. If the platform accepts video (most social networks do), keep the MP4 instead – it will look better and be a fraction of the size.

content.heading: How this converter keeps quality high
content.html: Instead of using a generic colour table, the converter runs two passes. The first pass scans your clip and builds a custom 256-colour palette (palettegen); the second pass maps every frame onto that palette with dithering (paletteuse). This avoids the blotchy banding you often see in GIFs made by simpler tools, especially on skin tones, gradients and skies.

content.heading: Tips for smaller GIFs
content.html: File size grows with width × height × frame count, so trimming is the most effective setting: use the start and end times to keep only the moment you need. 480 px wide and 10–12 fps look smooth enough for most uses. Busy, grainy footage compresses worse than flat screen recordings, so drop to the “Medium” or “Small file” quality if the result is too heavy for where you are posting it.

tools.title: MOV to MP4 Converter – Free, Private, No Upload
tools.description: Convert iPhone and QuickTime MOV videos to widely compatible MP4 (H.264 + AAC) in your browser. Optional trim and resize. Nothing is uploaded.
tools.lede: Convert QuickTime and iPhone MOV videos into MP4 files that play on Windows, Android, smart TVs and every web browser.

converter.tip: Conversion runs on your device's processor, so long 4K videos take a while. Choose 720p for a much faster conversion and a smaller file.

content.heading: MOV vs. MP4
content.html: MOV is Apple's QuickTime container and the default format for iPhone, iPad and many cameras and screen recorders. MP4 is the international standard (MPEG-4 Part 14) built on the same foundations. Both are only “boxes” – what matters is the video codec inside. iPhones usually record HEVC (H.265), which many Windows PCs, Android phones, older TVs and web browsers can't play without extra software.

content.heading: When to convert
content.html: Convert to MP4 when you need a video to “just work”: uploading to a website or LMS that rejects MOV, sharing with someone on Windows or Android, editing in software that doesn't support HEVC, or embedding on a web page. If you're staying inside the Apple ecosystem (Photos, iMovie, AirDrop to another iPhone), the original MOV is fine and slightly higher quality.

content.heading: What this converter produces
content.html: The output is H.264 video with AAC audio in an MP4 container – the most compatible combination there is. It uses the standard 8-bit colour format (yuv420p) that every player supports and moves the index to the start of the file (“fast start”), so the video begins playing online before it has fully downloaded. Phone rotation is applied automatically, so portrait videos stay upright.

content.heading: Tips
content.html: Everything is processed on your own device, so speed depends on your computer: a one-minute 1080p clip typically takes a minute or two on a modern laptop, longer on a phone. Use “720p” or trim the clip for faster results. “Balanced” quality is visually indistinguishable from the original for most footage. HDR (Dolby Vision) clips from recent iPhones are saved as a standard, non-HDR MP4 without tone-mapping, so colours may look slightly washed out compared with the phone screen; if that matters, turn off HDR video in the Camera settings before recording.

tools.title: MP4 to MP3 Converter – Extract Audio, No Upload
tools.description: Extract the audio from an MP4 video and save it as an MP3 at 128, 192 or 320 kbps. Runs in your browser – your video is never uploaded.
tools.lede: Pull the soundtrack out of an MP4 video and save it as an MP3 that plays on any phone, car stereo or music app.

converter.tip: Audio-only conversion is fast: most videos take a few seconds, because the picture is skipped entirely.

content.heading: MP4 vs. MP3
content.html: An MP4 file is a container that usually holds a video track plus an audio track (normally AAC). MP3 is an audio-only format, and the most widely supported one there is: it plays in every browser, phone, music app, car stereo, smart speaker and old MP3 player. Converting MP4 to MP3 throws away the picture and keeps just the sound, so the file is a small fraction of the video's size.

content.heading: When to extract the audio
content.html: Use this for recorded lectures, interviews, meetings, podcasts recorded on camera, voice memos saved as video, or a performance you want to listen to without the screen on. If you're keeping the audio inside the Apple ecosystem, the original AAC track is slightly more efficient – but if you need it to “just play” everywhere, MP3 is the safe choice.

content.heading: Choosing a bitrate
content.html: Bitrate sets how much data is used per second of sound. 128 kbps is plenty for speech and keeps files small (about 1 MB per minute). 192 kbps is a good default for music and sounds transparent to most listeners (about 1.4 MB per minute). 320 kbps is the MP3 maximum (about 2.4 MB per minute); use it for music you care about, but note it can't add back detail the original video's audio didn't have.

content.heading: Tips
content.html: Use the start and end times to grab just one song or answer from a long recording. The audio is re-encoded once, so for the best result convert from the original video rather than from a copy that has been through messaging apps. If you get a “no audio track” message, the video was recorded or exported without sound.

tools.title: WebM to MP4 Converter – Free, Private, No Upload
tools.description: Convert WebM videos (VP8/VP9, Opus) to MP4 with H.264 and AAC so they play on iPhone, Windows and in video editors. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.lede: Turn WebM screen recordings and downloads into MP4 files that play on iPhones, in PowerPoint and in every video editor.

converter.tip: Conversion runs on your device's processor. Screen recordings convert quickly; long HD videos take a few minutes.

content.heading: WebM vs. MP4
content.html: WebM is an open, royalty-free video format from Google, using the VP8 or VP9 (sometimes AV1) video codecs with Vorbis or Opus audio. It's what you get from many screen recorders, browser recording tools, OBS presets and some downloaders. MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio is the most compatible combination in existence: it plays on iPhones and iPads, in QuickTime, PowerPoint and Keynote, on TVs and in virtually every editing program.

content.heading: When to convert
content.html: Convert when a WebM won't open where you need it: an iPhone or older Mac, a video editor such as iMovie or Premiere that refuses the file, a presentation, a learning platform, or a site that only accepts MP4 uploads. If the video is only going to be played on a website in a modern browser, WebM is fine as it is – browsers all support it.

content.heading: What this converter produces
content.html: Video is re-encoded to H.264 with the standard 8-bit yuv420p colour format, which phones, TVs and hardware players require; audio becomes AAC. Width and height are rounded down to even numbers if needed (H.264 requires it), and the index is placed at the start of the file so it streams immediately. Transparency in WebM files (used for stickers and overlays) is not supported by H.264 and will be lost.

content.heading: Picking a quality
content.html: “Balanced” (CRF 23) looks the same as the source for most material. Screen recordings with lots of flat colour compress very well, so “Smaller file” is often indistinguishable for tutorials and demos. Choose “Higher quality” for camera footage with fine detail. Converting can't improve quality: the MP4 will be at best as sharp as the WebM you start with, and is often a little larger, because VP9 is a more efficient codec than H.264.

tools.title: GIF to MP4 Converter – Shrink Animated GIFs, No Upload
tools.description: Convert animated GIFs to MP4 (H.264) videos that are often 5–20× smaller and post anywhere. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
tools.lede: Turn an animated GIF into an MP4 video that's typically a small fraction of the size, ready for Instagram, websites and messaging apps.

converter.tip: GIFs have no sound, so the MP4 is silent. Most social apps will still loop a short MP4 automatically.

content.heading: GIF vs. MP4
content.html: GIF is a 1987 image format that can hold a sequence of frames, each limited to 256 colours, with no sound. MP4 is a modern video format; here it holds H.264 video, the codec used by nearly every phone, browser and streaming service. Both can show the same short loop, but they store it in completely different ways.

content.heading: Why the MP4 is so much smaller
content.html: A GIF saves every frame as its own picture, compressed only with simple lossless LZW compression, so 10 seconds of animation is essentially hundreds of separate images. H.264 compresses motion: it stores an occasional full frame and, for the frames in between, only what changed – which blocks moved and by how much. It also uses lossy compression tuned to what the eye actually notices. The result is commonly 5 to 20 times smaller than the GIF, and it can show millions of colours instead of 256, so gradients look smooth rather than speckled.

content.heading: When to use each
content.html: Keep the GIF where only images are allowed: email newsletters, some forums, GitHub READMEs and older chat tools. Use MP4 everywhere video works – Instagram and TikTok (which reject GIF uploads), websites (an autoplaying, muted, looping <video> loads far faster than a big GIF), slide decks and messaging apps. Your page speed, and your visitors' data plans, will thank you.

content.heading: Tips
content.html: H.264 needs even dimensions, so a GIF that's 501 × 301 px becomes 500 × 300 – a single pixel row or column is trimmed, nothing is stretched. Transparent areas become black, because MP4 has no transparency. Very small GIFs (under ~100 KB, a few frames) may not shrink much, as the MP4 container has a little fixed overhead. Choose “Higher quality” for pixel-art or text-heavy animations, which show compression artefacts more easily.
